lessons.title: Lesson 1: Budget basics: income, needs and wants
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List your monthly income and sort your spending into needs and wants.
This lesson builds toward: Given one month of pay stubs, statements or receipts, you will list your income and sort your expenses into needs and wants, with at least ten expenses, rounded amounts and totals.
A budget is a plan for your money. It shows what comes in each month and where it goes. A budget does not mean you can never have fun; it means you decide on purpose.
Income is money coming in: paychecks, benefits, child support, side jobs. Needs are things you must pay to live and work: rent, food, utilities, transportation, child care, medicine. Wants are nice to have: eating out, streaming, new clothes you do not need yet.
Start with one month. Look at pay stubs, bank or card statements and receipts. Round amounts to the nearest dollar or five dollars; close is good enough to start.
Step by step:
- Write every source of income for one month.
- List every expense you can remember or find.
- Mark each expense as a need or a want.
- Add up income, needs and wants.
Words to know:
- Budget: a plan for how you will use your money each month.
- Income: money coming in.
- Expense: money going out.
Try it now: On paper or in a free spreadsheet, write your monthly income and at least ten expenses. Mark each one N for need or W for want.
You can now list your income and sort expenses into needs and wants.

options: Money coming in, like paychecks and benefits
check.why: Income is money coming in, such as paychecks, benefits or side jobs.

check.q: You are listing expenses and pay about $87.60 for phone. What do you write to start?
options: Nothing until you find the exact cents
check.why: Rounding to the nearest dollar or five is good enough to start a budget.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Using AI to organize your budget safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask a free AI assistant to sort and explain your budget without sharing private information.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free AI assistant, you will organize your budget into a table and choose which of its suggestions fit your family, sharing only rounded categories and checking the totals with a calculator.
A free AI assistant such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot or Google Gemini can turn your list into a neat table, add it up, and point out where money is going. You stay in charge of every decision.
Share only rounded amounts and categories. Never type account numbers, card numbers, your Social Security number, passwords, or your bank's login. Example prompt: "My family of 4 brings in about $3,200 a month. Rent $1,400, food $650, phone $90, bus passes $100, eating out $200, streaming $40. Put this in a table, total it, and suggest two places we could cut back."
AI can make math mistakes. Add the totals yourself or with a calculator to check. Its tips are ideas, not rules; pick what fits your family.
Step by step:
- Write your categories and rounded amounts.
- Remove any account numbers or private details.
- Ask AI to make a table, total it and suggest cuts.
- Check the totals yourself.
- Choose which suggestions fit your family.
Words to know:
- Category: a group of spending, like food or transportation.
- Placeholder: a stand-in like "[my bank]" used instead of private details.
Try it now: Give an AI assistant your rounded categories and amounts (no private details). Ask for a table, a total and two ideas to cut back. Check the total with a calculator.
You can now use AI to organize a budget without sharing private information, and check its math.

check.q: Who makes the final choices about your budget when you use AI?
check.why: AI gives ideas, but you stay in charge of every decision.

check.q: You want AI to sort your budget. What do you type?
options: Your card number and its code
check.why: Only rounded amounts and categories go into the AI, never private numbers.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Setting a savings goal and keeping money safe
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set one savings goal with an amount and a date, and know how bank deposits are protected.
This lesson builds toward: Given something you want to save for, you will set a savings goal with an amount and a date, calculate the weekly amount and choose a safe place to keep it, with the math checked and an FDIC-insured bank or federally insured credit union.
Even a small amount saved each week can help when a car breaks down or hours get cut. Many people start with an emergency fund: money set aside only for surprises.
Make the goal clear: "Save $300 for emergencies by June 1." Divide by the number of weeks to see how much to set aside each week. Ask AI to do the math, then check it.
Where you keep savings matters. Money in a bank insured by the FDIC is protected up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, for each account ownership category. FDIC insurance does not cover stocks or crypto. Check that a bank is FDIC-insured on fdic.gov before you open an account.
Step by step:
- Choose what you are saving for.
- Pick an amount and a date.
- Divide the amount by the number of weeks.
- Keep savings in a federally insured bank or credit union.
Words to know:
- Emergency fund: money saved only for surprise costs.
- FDIC: the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, which protects money in insured banks.
- Credit union: a member-owned, not-for-profit financial institution.
Official sources:
- FDIC: Understanding Deposit Insurance
Try it now: Write one savings goal with an amount and a date. Work out how much to save each week, then ask AI to check your math.
You can now set a clear savings goal and choose a safe, insured place to keep it.

check.q: What makes a savings goal clear?
check.why: A clear goal says how much and by when, like $300 by June 1.

check.q: You want to save $200 in 20 weeks. How much do you set aside each week?
check.why: $200 divided by 20 weeks is $10 a week.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Credit, help and staying safe

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Checking your credit report for free
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find the official site for free credit reports and check a report for mistakes.
This lesson builds toward: Using AnnualCreditReport.com, you will explain how to get your free credit reports and check them for mistakes, naming the three bureaus and what to dispute.
A credit report is a record of your loans, cards and bills. Landlords, lenders and some employers may look at it. Mistakes happen, and a mistake can cost you an apartment or a loan.
You can get free credit reports from the three big credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, every week at AnnualCreditReport.com. That is the official site. Other sites that promise "free" reports may try to sell you something.
Look for accounts you do not recognize, wrong addresses and late payments you did make on time. If something is wrong, you can dispute it with the credit bureau. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau at consumerfinance.gov explains how.
Step by step:
- Type AnnualCreditReport.com yourself in the browser.
- Request your reports from Equifax, Experian and TransUnion.
- Look for accounts you do not know, wrong details and wrong late payments.
- If something is wrong, follow the dispute steps on consumerfinance.gov.
Words to know:
- Credit report: a record of your loans, credit cards and bill payments.
- Credit bureau: a company that keeps credit reports: Equifax, Experian, TransUnion.
- Dispute: officially ask to fix a mistake.
Official sources:
- FTC: Free Credit Reports
- Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: Consumer tools
Try it now: Write down the official site for free credit reports and the three bureau names. If you are ready and on a private device, request one report and look for anything you do not recognize.
You can now get your free credit reports from the official site and spot mistakes to dispute.

check.q: Who may look at your credit report?
check.why: Landlords, lenders and some employers may check your credit report.

check.q: An ad offers a "free" credit report on a site you do not know. What do you do?
options: Sign up and enter your card
check.why: AnnualCreditReport.com is the official site; others may try to sell you something.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Free tax and money help
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find a free tax help site and a trusted source for money questions.
This lesson builds toward: When you need tax or money help, you will find a free VITA or TCE tax site and a trusted source for money questions, writing down the site's address and what to bring.
You do not need to pay a lot to get your taxes done. The IRS Volunteer Income Tax Assistance program, VITA, gives free tax help, mostly to people who meet the Earned Income Tax Credit income guidelines. Many sites also help people who make about $70,244 or less, people with disabilities and people with limited English. Each site can set its own rules, so check with the site.
Find a VITA site with the IRS VITA/TCE Locator at freetaxassistance.for.irs.gov or by calling 800-906-9887. TCE gives similar free help, mainly to people 60 and older.
For other money questions, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau at consumerfinance.gov has free guides on bank accounts, debt collection, payday loans and more, and a way to submit a complaint about a company. Payday loans and quick-cash apps can cost far more than they seem; read the full cost before you sign.
Step by step:
- Search the IRS VITA/TCE Locator or call 800-906-9887.
- Ask the site what to bring.
- Use consumerfinance.gov for money questions.
- Before any loan, ask for the full cost in dollars.
Words to know:
- VITA: Volunteer Income Tax Assistance: free IRS-backed tax help.
- Payday loan: a small, short-term loan that can be very expensive.
Official sources:
- IRS: Free tax return preparation for qualifying taxpayers
- Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: Consumer tools
Try it now: Use the IRS VITA/TCE Locator to find the free tax help site nearest you. Write down its address and what it says to bring.
You can now find free tax help and trusted money information.

options: Free tax help, mainly for people 60 and older
check.why: TCE gives free tax help like VITA, mainly to people 60 and older.

check.q: A quick-cash app offers you $200 today. What do you ask first?
options: How fast you can get more
check.why: Payday loans and quick-cash apps can cost far more than they seem.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Spotting money scams, and your final plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Spot common money scams and finish your budget plan.
This lesson builds toward: Given a money offer or urgent message, you will spot the warning signs of a money scam and choose the safe next step, sharing no logins or codes and reporting scams to the FTC.
Scammers go after people who are short on money with fake loans, fake debt relief, fake government grants and "get rich quick" offers, including crypto schemes. Some now use AI to write real-looking messages or copy a family member's voice.
Warning signs: they rush you, ask you to pay with gift cards, wire transfers, payment apps or crypto, promise guaranteed money, or ask for your bank login or the code sent to your phone. A real government agency will not call and demand payment that way.
If something feels wrong, stop, hang up and call back using a number you know is real. You can report scams to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Step by step:
- Watch for rushing, gift cards, crypto and guaranteed money.
- Never share bank logins or phone codes.
- Hang up and call back on a number you know.
- Report scams to the FTC.
Words to know:
- Scam: a trick to steal money or information.
- Guaranteed returns: a promise that you will surely make money; a common scam line.
Official sources:
- Federal Trade Commission: ReportFraud.ftc.gov
Try it now: Final task: finish your one-month budget with AI help (no private numbers), check the totals, write one savings goal with an amount and date, and write where you will get your free credit report and free tax help.
You can now make a household budget, plan savings, find free help and avoid money scams.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Budget Income or expenses missing, or needs and wants not marked. One month of income and expenses with rounded amounts, each marked need or want, and totals. Uses pay stubs, statements or receipts to make the amounts close. AI used safely The prompt has an account, card or Social Security number, or totals were not checked. Only rounded categories shared, totals checked, and one place to save chosen. Explains why they kept or rejected each AI suggestion. Savings goal No amount or date. One goal with an amount, a date and a checked weekly amount. Names where the money will be kept and that it is federally insured. Credit report and tax help Does not say where to get the report or tax help. Names AnnualCreditReport.com and a VITA or TCE site to use. Has the tax site's address and what to bring. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which payment request is a scam warning sign?
options: A bill from your known utility at its usual address
Paying rent to your landlord by check
Being told to pay with gift cards
check.why: Scammers ask for gift cards, wire transfers, payment apps or crypto.

check.q: You get a call in your cousin's voice asking for money right now. What do you do?
options: Hang up and call your cousin on a number you know
check.why: Scammers can copy voices with AI, so you call back on a known number.
